items.title: Differentiable Spin-Center Diffusion Model Enables DEER-Guided Generative Pipeline of Weighted Protein Ensembles
items.abstract_or_text: Biological function entails the interconversion of a protein between distinct conformations, an equilibrium modulated by ligands and other physicochemical conditions. Double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy captures these ensembles as distance distributions, P(r), between spin label pairs. However, the width of P(r) convolves protein conformational heterogeneity with the rotameric flexibility of the label. Because current spin label models overestimate this contribution, translating P(r) into ensembles has remained indirect and predominantly qualitative. Here, we developed spin-center (SC) diffusion, a differentiable model of the spin label with a tunable spin label rotameric width. Coupled to a frozen Boltz-2 structure generator, SC diffusion enables the entire experimental P(r) to guide ensemble generation at inference time. We demonstrate the robustness of this pipeline on synthetic P(r) of known composition, recovering the ensemble populations, including both components of a bimodal profile. Guided by experimental P(r) measured under different biochemical conditions, ensembles of the transporters PfMATE, LmrP, MhsT and P-glycoprotein were modeled and free energy differences derived from the ensembles in a condition-dependent manner. By embedding a differentiable label model in structure generation, our approach interprets DEER distributions as weighted conformational ensembles, adding a missing thermodynamic grounding to generative protein structure prediction methods.

items.title: 3DRISM Solvation for Accurate and Large-Scale Protein Hydration Prediction and Mechanistic Interpretation
items.abstract_or_text: Solvation plays essential roles in protein stability, molecular recognition, and enzyme catalysis. The three-dimensional reference interaction site model (3DRISM), an integral equation theory of molecular solvation, provides an attractive balance between computational efficiency and predictive accuracy by explicitly predicting 3-dimensional hydration structures while avoiding the costly sampling required by explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. However, its performance for protein-wide hydration prediction has not been systematically evaluated across a large and diverse set of protein structures, particularly in comparison with recent machine learning (ML) approaches. Here, we systematically benchmark 3DRISM against the state-of-the-art ML model, SuperWater, across its Train and Test datasets and an independently constructed Query dataset of 3,139 protein structures outside its training domain. Across these datasets, 3DRISM achieves hydration-site prediction accuracy comparable to SuperWater. 3DRISM calculations performed with our EPISOL software package remain computationally efficient for large-scale applications. Comparison with explicit-solvent MD simulations of 20 randomly selected proteins further demonstrates that 3DRISM accurately reproduces equilibrium solvent density distributions across diverse local protein environments. Finally, using the periplasmic binding protein SiaP as a case study, we show that the solvent density predicted by 3DRISM directly captures mutationinduced solvent depletion within a buried ligand-binding pocket, and accurately reconstructs the corresponding water positions involved in the hydrogen-bond network. By directly computing the equilibrium solvent distribution, 3DRISM provides mechanistic insight into ligand recognition by revealing hydration changes that are difficult to capture using conventional explicit-solvent MD simulations potentially due to the slow water exchange in the buried binding pocket. Our results establish 3DRISM as an accurate, computationally efficient, and mechanistically informative framework for large-scale protein hydration prediction.

items.title: SolviScope: An Interaction-Aware Graph Neural Network for Solvent Ranking of Small Organic Molecules in Pure and Multicomponent Solvent Systems
items.abstract_or_text: Selecting effective solvents and antisolvents requires navigating vast chemical, composition, and temperature spaces where exhaustive experimentation is prohibitively costly and low average regression errors do not guarantee that the best candidates appear within a short experimental screen. We introduce SolviScope, a graph neural network framework for solubility prediction and solvent ranking in pure and binary solvent systems. SolviScope-Pure combines a two-dimensional gated graph encoder with intermolecular cross-attention, avoiding three-dimensional conformer generation. SolviScope-Binary integrates hierarchical message passing with Kamlet–Taft and Hansen descriptors and temperature–composition conditioning. Both models use explicit ranking objectives. SolviScope-Pure achieves a molar logS root-mean-square error of 0.77 on a 7,264-measurement structural hold-out set, lower errors than FastSolv on two overlap-filtered external benchmarks, and better solvent-ranking correlations for 8 of 10 industrially relevant solutes. Across two industrial mixture benchmarks comprising 13 solutes, SolviScope-Binary achieves per-solute Spearman’s ρ of 0.51–0.91 and recovers the experimentally most and least soluble systems within its top-five and bottom-five predictions for every solute. Retrospective studies of two unseen APIs further demonstrate solvent/antisolvent prioritization and correct composition ordering in solvent–water mixtures. Cooling-crystallization assessments reveal that successful isothermal ranking does not establish reliable cooling-drop ranking or quantitative working-capacity prediction. These results support SolviScope as a tool for prioritizing experimental solvent screens, with prospective validation needed to establish broader applicability and experimental savings.

items.title: Identification and Experimental Validation of Repurposable Drugs Targeting the Essential ClpP1 Protease of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
items.abstract_or_text: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health challenge, necessitating the identification of novel therapeutic targets and accelerated drug discovery strategies. The caseinolytic protease (ClpP) complex of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is essential for proteostasis, stress adaptation, and bacterial survival, making it an attractive yet underexplored drug target. Comparative structural analysis also revealed significant differences between mycobacterial and human ClpP S1 pockets, suggesting opportunities for selective inhibition. In this study, a structure-based drug repurposing approach was employed to identify approved drugs targeting the S1 pocket of the ClpP1 subunit, a key regulatory site involved in proteolytic activation. Virtual screening of the approved drug library against the ClpP1 crystal structure (PDB ID: 4U0G) identified Saquinavir and Raltegravir as the most promising candidates, exhibiting binding affinities of –9.1 and –9.5 kcal/mol, respectively, and favorable interactions with critical S1 pocket residues. Molecular dynamics simulations over 200 ns confirmed stable ligand binding and persistent occupancy within the S1 pocket. In vitro evaluation against M. tuberculosis H37Ra demonstrated potent concentration-dependent antimycobacterial activity, with Saquinavir showing superior efficacy (IC50 = 0.01 ± 0.007 μM; MIC = 64 μM) compared with Raltegravir (IC50 = 0.1 ± 0.09 μM; MIC ≥ 128 μM). Growth kinetics, REMA, and statistical analyses further validated their inhibitory activity. These findings validate Saquinavir and Raltegravir as potential repurposable anti-tubercular agents for further mechanistic and preclinical evaluation.

items.title: Construction of a Curated Literature Dataset and Machine Learning-Guided Exploration of Supported Metal Catalysts for Low- to Intermediate-Temperature Reverse Water–Gas Shift Reaction
items.abstract_or_text: Literature-derived results on reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) catalysts contain extensive information about catalyst design, yet their fragmentation makes systematic, data-driven exploration difficult. Here, we establish a framework that connects a curated RWGS literature dataset to interpretable machine-learning (ML) models and a flexible catalyst-search algorithm. We compiled 607 experimental records from 42 publications on supported metal and metal oxide catalysts evaluated at 300–450 °C, integrating catalyst compositions, preparation and reaction conditions, and CO yields. By systematically comparing nine regression algorithms and nine input representations, we obtained mean cross-validated test R2 values of 0.80, 0.73, and 0.58 for models optimized for the full, 300 °C, and 400 °C datasets, respectively. SHAP analysis identified compositional and experimental features contributing to model predictions, while leave-one-out validation exposed substantial prediction errors in some literature records. In offline sequential-search simulations repeated 100 times, ML-guided search identified high-yield literature entries more efficiently than random selection. Importantly, our newly developed Local-search algorithm jointly explored elemental combinations, loadings, support materials, and experimental conditions without exhaustive enumeration, generating candidates beyond the compositions represented in the training data. The 300 °C search favored Pt–Na/ZrO2-containing candidates, whereas Pd–Na/CeO2-containing candidates predominated at 400 °C. Although these predictions await experimental validation and some violate RWGS equilibrium constraints, this integrated framework provides a reusable data resource and a practical route from accumulated literature knowledge to testable catalyst-design hypotheses.

items.title: ETALON: Verified Execution and Persistent Research Memory for Agentic Computer-Aided Drug Design
items.abstract_or_text: Language-model agents can coordinate computational drug discovery, but adapting a campaign to new evidence requires scientific software that supports flexible workflows, consistent modeling, and continuity across research sessions. Here we present ETALON, a harness that equips a general-purpose coding agent with an integrated environment for computer-aided drug design. Three independently usable systems supply its scientific operations: MolQuarry for chemical and biological evidence, MolCascade for molecular preparation, screening, and docking, and PRISM for molecular generation and physical modeling. Each exposes configurable procedures with explicit scientific requirements, so the host can revise its research strategy while retaining consistent preparation and evaluation practices. Operations registered with a common execution layer are checked before dispatch, and their outputs carry separate records of completion, verification, and admission, so that an incomplete computation is not recorded as an unfavorable molecular result. A persistent research graph links evidence, judgments, experiments, and results across sessions, and candidate method revisions are compared with frozen baselines under criteria declared in advance.

items.title: Ensemble of ∆-ML Models for Quantum Chemistry Level of Theory Selection for Interaction Energies
items.abstract_or_text: Ab initio quantum chemical approaches for computing interactions between molecules are useful in a wide range of applications but can be difficult to apply effectively. In particular, variations in cost and accuracy across different levels of theory (method and basis set combinations) makes it challenging to select an appropriate level of theory for a given chemical system. In this work, we train ∆-machine learning models to predict interaction energy errors for 81 levels of theory versus a reference and simple polynomial models to quantify computational cost for a meaningful subset of these methods. We demonstrate how a large language model (LLM) can leverage these models to select appropriate levels of theory and run computations autonomously on distributed resources, significantly reducing the barrier to obtaining accurate interaction energies.

items.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
items.abstract_or_text: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships1. Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

items.title: Diffusion-Based Synthetic Pretraining for Root Segmentation in Rhizotron Images
items.abstract_or_text: Rhizotrons allow root system architecture to be studied non-destructively in soil. However, automated analysis of rhizotron images remains difficult: roots have low contrast against soil, soil particles resemble fine roots, and deep learning models need many manually annotated images that are slow and subjective to produce. Synthetic images could provide paired images and annotations at scale, but rhizotron images are largely absent from the data used to train generative models. We built a pipeline combining Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), ControlNet and inpainting to generate synthetic rhizotron images with paired root masks. We compared training on synthetic data only, real data only, and synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on real images, using three segmentation models: nnU-Net v2, YOLO26 and Mask2Former. Synthetic-only training reached a Dice score of up to 0.60. Synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the full real training set (two annotated rhizotron images) reached 0.80, and nnU-Net v2 and Mask2Former reached 0.62 with only two annotated image patches containing visible roots. When real annotations were limited, pretraining also improved segmentation of unseen crops, including lettuce, barley, wheat, maize, tomato, cucumber, French bean and field bean. We also introduced a Soft Dice score that compares predictions with probabilistic consensus maps from seven independent annotators, accounting for annotator disagreement. Models matched average human agreement on low-ambiguity patches but remained below it on high-ambiguity patches. In conclusion, diffusion-generated images can complement real annotations and help scale root segmentation, although their effect on downstream root trait measurements still needs to be validated.

items.title: Materials Property Prediction with a Site-Resolved Three-Dimensional Voxel Convolution Neural Network
items.abstract_or_text: Identifying low-energy atomic arrangements is central to the design of multicomponent materials such as high-entropy cathodes and perovskites, but the number of possible arrangements grows combinatorially with the number of elements. Calculating each arrangement with density functional theory (DFT) is impractical, and many machine-learning models require relaxed structures that become available only after such calculations. This study presents a site-resolved voxel three-dimensional convolutional neural network (SiVox) that maps each crystallographic site of a known prototype onto a voxel and encodes the occupying element by its physicochemical properties, so that only the site assignment is required as input. The model was evaluated on 1,287,000 configurations of high-entropy Li-rich layered oxides (HE-LLOs) and 18,928 cubic ABX3 perovskites. For HE-LLOs, it reached configurational R2 values of 0.989 for new configurations of training compositions and 0.993 for compositions excluded from training, compared with 0.92–0.93 for descriptor-based models. For perovskites, site assignment alone lowered the formation-energy MAE from 0.432 to 0.133 eV/cell relative to composition descriptors, and screening about 6% of the candidates recovered 90% of the lowest-energy 5%. Relaxed lattice parameters and atomic displacements reduced the error further and mattered most when the most stable of seven anion variants had to be identified. These results indicate that site assignment on a known framework is sufficient to narrow a large candidate space before structural relaxation.

items.title: Integrating Generative AI and Data Science into General Chemistry Laboratories
items.abstract_or_text: The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

items.title: PROBE-Select: A Web Server for Selecting Optimal Protein-Specific Labeling Reagents to Maximize Structural Information Obtained from Covalent Labeling Mass Spectrometry
items.abstract_or_text: Covalent labeling mass spectrometry (CL-MS) reports the solvent exposure of individual residues, but how much structural information an experiment returns depends on which labeling reagent is used. Currently, there are no tools available to guide the reagent choice. Here, we present PROBE-Select (PRotein-Oriented Best-reagent Evaluator for Selective labeling), a computational workflow that selects labeling reagents for a given protein sequence and is available as a web application on the Rosetta Online Server that Includes Everyone (ROSIE). Starting from a sequence, the workflow generates a ColabFold ensemble of candidate structures under diversity-promoting settings, removes models dominated by nonregular secondary structure, clusters the remaining models, and selects three representative conformations. The workflow then retains as reporters all residues whose predicted solvent exposure differs between at least two of the three representatives by more than a threshold T. Reporters are mapped to compatible labeling reagents, and each reagent is scored by the number of reporters it can label for each conformation pair. On a benchmark of 11 proteins with experimentally characterized alternative conformations, the workflow identified 182 reporter residues at T = 5. The number of reporters increased with the structural separation between representatives, and the number of reporters available to each reagent differed between proteins and between pairs of representatives. Diethylpyrocarbonate was the top-ranked residue-selective reagent in 8 of the 10 benchmark proteins that had reporters. PROBE-Select returns the reagent ranking, the residue-level exposure data behind it, and the three representative structures. PROBE-Select is freely available for academic and non-profit use, and can be accessed with a GitHub account via this link ( r2.graylab.jhu.edu/apps/submit/probe-select ).

items.title: Regioselective sugar epimerization to rare sugar on ruthenium surface
items.abstract_or_text: Rare sugars, monosaccharides that occur only rarely in nature, exhibit physicochemical and biological properties distinct from those of naturally abundant sugars such as D-glucose. Their widespread utilization has been hindered by limitations in existing production methods, which rely primarily on equilibrium-constrained biocatalytic cascades or on synthetic approaches requiring multiple steps or organic reagents. Here we show the one-pot heterogeneous catalytic epimerization of methyl glucosides into rare sugar derivatives over supported Ru catalysts under hydrogen atmosphere in water. Among the supported metals examined, Ru uniquely promotes regioselective stereoinversion of 1- O -methyl β-D-glucopyranoside at the C3 position to produce 1- O -methyl β-D-allopyranoside without requiring additional reagents or multistep reactions. Isotopelabeling experiments reveal that dehydrogenation and hydrogenation proceed substantially faster than net epimerization, identifying surface-confined molecular rotation of a keto intermediate as the rate-determining step. Computer simulations further show that the experimentally observed regioselectivity originates from the low rotational free energy barriers and relatively high stability of the keto intermediate on the Ru surface. These findings identify molecular rotational dynamics on catalyst surfaces as a governing principle for stereochemical inversion reactions.

items.title: vibe-qc: expert-directed agentic engineering for scientific software development
items.abstract_or_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can implement scientific software, but useful development also requires executable comparisons, inspectable results and a record of scientific decisions. This case study examines the tooling that enables semi-autonomous electronic-structure software development under expert direction. VIBE-QC supplies molecular and periodic calculations; vibe-scheduler queues and manages calculations across clusters and a fleet of workstations; vibe-viewer and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) connect numerical outputs to portable inspection and reproducible figures. Retained development records illustrate how these tools preserve failed attempts, distinguish changes in physical conventions from implementation errors, and separate measured differences from expert-selected acceptance criteria. Publication-specific calculations were run with VIBE-QC 0.18.x and use formaldehyde to connect controlled numerical comparisons with visual inspection; diamond and lithium hydride provide periodic Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) examples with explicit convergence checks. The expert sets the physical problem, selects diagnostic controls and interprets the evidence; AI agents implement and execute those tasks. The resulting account identifies practical requirements for sustained AI-assisted scientific development. It establishes a traceable process within one project, without claiming autonomous scientific judgment or a measured productivity advantage.

items.title: TS Second Opinion: catching, repairing and triaging mirror-image errors in machine-learned transition states
items.abstract_or_text: Generative models now predict a reaction’s transition state (TS) in milliseconds, but they cannot say when a guess is wrong. On the RDB7 benchmark, 17.7% of the TS guesses from GoFlow, a flow-matching TS generator, have a stereocentre the wrong way round, and 85% of those still count as accurate by the usual distance-based score. 90% of these errors are whole mirror images, which have the same energy and vibrational frequencies as the correct TS, so they also pass a frequency check. We present TS Second Opinion, a model-agnostic layer that runs after generation. Chemists state checks in plain English; a large language model (Claude) writes each check as Python, and a gate keeps it only if it accepts at least 99% of 9,540 reference DFT transition states, never crashes, and still catches mirrored or distorted ones. The accepted checks then test every guess, repair whole mirror images by reflection, and assign each reaction a verdict (trust, check with DFT, or re-generate); conformal selection turns the ranking into a set of trusted reactions with a stated average error rate. On 1,194 held-out RDB7 reactions with eight GoFlow models, two LLM-written stereo checks catch 93% of wrong-handed guesses at 0.2% false alarms, wrong-handed final answers fall from 17.7% to 2.3%, and 80% of reactions can be trusted at a 5% average geometry-error rate. New ωB97X/def2-SVP transition-state optimisations on 16 reactions support both the symmetry argument and the verdicts: an unrepaired mirror image converges to a first-order saddle point 0.0006 kcal/mol from the repaired one, all six trusted guesses reach the reference TS, and none of the six re-generate guesses do, although five of them still pass a DFT frequency check. The results are mostly retrospective, on one dataset and one model family; code, data and a browser app are openly available.

items.title: Machine learning–driven inverse design of nanofiltration membranes for selective Mg2+/Na+ separation
items.abstract_or_text: Desalination brine, a byproduct of seawater desalination, contains valuable resources, including magnesium. Recovering magnesium requires selectively retaining Mg 2+ while allowing the dominant monovalent cation, Na + , to permeate. Nanofiltration (NF) membranes fabricated by interfacial polymerization are promising for this Mg 2+ /Na + separation, but their performance depends on coupled formulation and processing variables that are inefficient to optimize through trial and error. Here, we demonstrate a workflow integrating dataset curation, forward prediction, and inverse design of thin-film composite NF membranes. A dataset of 1,253 entries, comprising literature and in-house records, was cleaned, imputed, and augmented through chemically constrained permutation of interchangeable polymer, solvent, and salt variables in the training split only. Optimized extremely randomized tree regressors predicted pure water permeability, solute rejection, and intermediate membrane properties, achieving test-set coefficients of determination above 0.79. Shapley analysis indicated that permeability was governed primarily by formulation and processing variables, whereas rejection depended mainly on solute identity and charge, as well as membrane tightness. Using Bayesian optimization with a scalarized objective, two membrane recipes with favorable Mg 2+ /Na + selectivity were identified and experimentally validated. The inversely designed membranes exhibited the required Mg 2+ /Na + selectivity, demonstrating the capability of this workflow to design Mg 2+ -selective NF membranes for resource recovery from desalination brine.

items.title: Incorporating Polarization into ML/MM Endpoint Calculations for Protein–Ligand Affinity Ranking
items.abstract_or_text: Endpoint free-energy calculations combine low computational cost with reasonable accuracy and are widely used to rank protein–ligand affinities, yet describing charge polarization in these calculations remains a challenge. Here we introduce a machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) framework that incorporates polarizationcorrected mechanical embedding (PCME) and electrostatic embedding (EE) into endpoint calculations, using binding-state-and conformation-dependent ML charges in both the gas-phase energy and polar solvation terms. On a benchmark of 15 targets from the JACS and Merck sets, the PCME and EE routes of ML/MM-PBSA rank affinities better than classical MM-PBSA, raising the median Spearman ρ from 0.216 to 0.343 and 0.329, respectively, at an acceptable computational cost. A charge-source control and the analysis of a representative PTP1B complex show how conformationdependent ML charges resolve asymmetric local electrostatic environments and contribute to the improved ranking of ML/MM-PBSA(PCME) over MM-PBSA. By incorporating charge redistribution into both interaction and solvation energies, this work provides a practical ML/MM endpoint framework for protein–ligand affinity ranking and analysis of the underlying electrostatic contributions.

items.title: Microbial Pyrolysis for the Sustainable Synthesis of Nanoparticle-Embedded Carbon Electrocatalysts
items.abstract_or_text: Electrocatalytic processes are essential for a sustainable global economy, yet conventional catalyst synthesis often relies on hazardous reagents and insulating binders that impede performance. Here, microbial extracellular electron transfer for nanoparticle synthesis is integrated with the controlled pyrolysis of microbial monolayers to generate nanoparticle-embedded carbon electrodes. Surface immobilization of Shewanella oneidensis using DNA "Velcro" yields uniform single-microbe-thick layers that are readily patterned and converted into conductive, turbostratic carbon films at temperatures between 800 °C and 1,100 °C. These bio-derived films exhibit progressive graphitic ordering and reach a minimum sheet resistance of 1.49 kΩ/sq, approaching the performance of pyrolyzed synthetic photoresists. Moreover, by leveraging the intrinsic biosynthetic capabilities of S. oneidensis, 3-5 nm palladium nanoparticles are formed directly on the cell surface and seamlessly integrated into the carbon matrix upon pyrolysis. These composites reduce the hydrogen evolution reaction overpotential by 100 mV. This bottom-up bioengineering approach is anticipated to enable the sustainable, programmable fabrication of next-generation electrocatalysts for diverse energy conversion applications.

items.title: Built in Minutes, Checked by Script: Instructor-Made Interactive Chemistry Study Guides with Generative AI
items.abstract_or_text: Interactive study guides, with practice problems that change every time, help on request and small simulations, are valuable and slow to build; few instructors have time to make one for every unit. I describe a workflow that lets one instructor, a chemist with no programming background, build such guides with a generative AI coding assistant in about ten minutes each, plus about half an hour of polishing, and deliver them through GitHub Pages to Canvas or D2L Brightspace. Twenty pages for General Chemistry I, a course for non-science majors, biochemistry and Organic Chemistry I illustrate it; seventeen were built with this workflow over about a month. Each guide is a single web page that runs in any current browser, needs no account and sends nothing to a server. The guides share a design: a roadmap of the topic, sections in teaching order, problems whose numbers change each time, feedback on wrong answers, and small virtual instruments such as a titration, a calorimeter and a thin-layer plate; nine offer three levels of help. The biochemistry and organic guides take their values from named textbooks, and a check of every page, which ran about 1.6 million generated problems and recomputed each answer independently, found no wrong answer key but did find faults that reading had missed: named mistakes accepted as correct, correct answers rejected, an answer given away, and physically impossible setups; all were fixed and the check run again. No learning outcomes are claimed; evaluation is future work.

items.title: XinPilot: a chemist-designed open‑source desktop workspace for traceable high-throughput synthesis and purity analysis
items.abstract_or_text: High-throughput chemistry enables parallel exploration of multiple reactions. But it often involves manual operations and the handling of data inputs and outputs across synthesis and analytical instruments that use different software and file formats. Automating high-throughput synthesis and purity analysis requires seamless information transfer throughout the process. Existing digital chemistry tools offer powerful capabilities for experiment design, automation, data management, and analysis; however, laboratories commonly rely on a combination of these tools rather than a single integrated platform. To streamline data transfer between the instruments used for synthesis (Tecan Liquid Handler), workup (Opentrons Liquid Handler), and purity analysis (Waters ACQUITY HPLC and QDa MS) at the Acceleration Consortium’s Medicinal Chemistry Self Driving Lab, we developed a workspace, XinPilot. XinPilot addresses this project-level interoperability problem through a chemist-designed Windows desktop workspace that brings together chemical stock information, synthesis records, reaction schemes, expected products, and analytical evidence within a portable project. Working alongside existing instrument-control systems, XinPilot generates worklists for the Tecan Fluent and Opentrons Flex and OT2 liquid handlers, records manual reagent additions, and imports transfer records from other liquid-handling workflows in Excel, CSV, and JSON-compatible formats. These results can be combined into a unified reaction map when they use the same plate format. Chemical IDs and reaction-to-analysis well mappings preserve the relationships among reaction compositions, expected products, and analytical samples. Integrated PyParse-based analysis allows chemists to inspect UV chromatograms, mass spectra, and integrated peaks. Chemists can also reassign product peaks for individual experiments while retaining the automated assignments for other experiments, without requiring coding knowledge. Experimental records, original imported files, and supported analytical inspection data can be retained in portable .xinpilot.zip projects for subsequent review, handover, and synthesis planning. An experimentally executed Suzuki–Miyaura campaign combining Tecan dispensing, manual additions, Opentrons aqueous workup and LC-MS review is presented as a tutorial-style demonstration of the workflow. Additional experimental examples independently performed by other chemists are provided in the Supporting Information. A separate demonstration uses published experimental data from 192 Chemspeed reactions. These data were converted into XinPilot-compatible transfer records and imported into two projects. Reaction structures were also generated using XinPilot's Cheminformatics tools, and both projects were exported as portable .xinpilot.zip files. Overall, XinPilot provides an integrated open‑source workspace for generating worklists for parallel synthesis and workup using Tecan and Opentron liquid handlers, facilitating the purity analysis and maintaining traceable links between experimental conditions, reaction products, and analytical results.

items.title: Convergent genome- and gene-level constraints shape repeated environmental adaptation in grasses
items.abstract_or_text: Grasses (Poaceae) dominate terrestrial ecosystems and sustain global food security, yet the genomic principles enabling their repeated adaptation to extreme environments remain unresolved. Combining dense phylogenomic sampling, global environmental data, and genomic large language models (gLLMs), we characterize the mutational targets underlying environmental shift across 687 genomes from 561 species spanning 17 climate zones. We identify 17-30 phylogenetically independent transitions into extreme temperature, water, and soil environments, accompanied by convergent shifts in genome-scale molecular properties, including the Nitrogen-to-Carbon balance and the biosynthetic cost of the proteome. Our gLLMs-informed phylogenetic mixed modeling framework identifies 330 genes that repeatedly associated with distinct axes of environmental variation, highlighting the importance of protein modification and localization within extracellular and organellar compartments. Overlaying independent convergent selection tests identifies 27 high-confidence candidates for further characterization. Together, our results show that grass adaptation is canalized by layered constraints at genome-wide and gene-specific scales, producing predictable evolutionary trajectories.

items.title: Single Molecule Diffusion Studies Reveal Rapid Translations Across Target Membrane Surfaces for both p40Phox PX domain and Class III PI3K VPS34 Complex 1, the Autophagy Lipid Kinase
items.abstract_or_text: Single molecule analyses are providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms by which peripheral membrane proteins approach and translate across a target bilayer surface before stable docking. Here we compare and contrast the translational movements of four diffusers on a representative supported lipid bilayer: (i) the fluorescent lipid LRB-(DO)PE, (ii) the G-protein Rab1A anchored to (DO)PE; (iii) the PI(3)P sensor p40Phox PX domain, and (iv) the autophagy lipid kinase VPS34 Complex 1. The latter enzyme is a Class III PI-3-Kinase and its unusual architecture exhibits two distinct membrane-docking "feet" unique to Class III PI3Ks. Notably, the membrane contact surfaces of the PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase each possess multiple positive charges suitable for electrostatic interactions with their anionic target membrane. The present single molecule tracking studies reveal that both the fluorescent lipid and the lipid-anchored G protein Rab1A exhibit 2-dimensional translation typical of simple lipid diffusion in the bilayer. Single molecule density measurements indicate both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit significantly reduced membrane docking when the bilayer negative charge is decreased, confirming the importance of their protein-bilayer electrostatic interactions. Single molecule tracking studies reveal that both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit hopping movements across the bilayer surface during their initial bilayer contacts, yielding a significantly higher frequency of long range displacements than allowed by lipid 2-D diffusion. After transitioning from hopping to a stable bilayer-docked state, both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit 2-D diffusion slower than lipid diffusion indicating the appearance of increased frictional drag against the bilayer due to new protein-bilayer contacts. PX domain requires its target lipid for the transition from electrostatic hopping to stable bilayer docking, while autophagy lipid kinase can dock spontaneously to anionic lipid bilayers even in the absence of its substrate lipid. In principle, the slowly diffusing, bilayer-docked states of PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase could be interrupted by unbinding-hopping-rebinding events. However, such events are not detected for PX domain in the presence of target lipid (DO)PI(3)P nor for autophagy lipid kinase in the presence of substrate lipid (DO)PI. Instead, unbinding-hopping-rebinding events are only observed for autophagy lipid kinase in the absence of substrate lipid, indicating that the presence of a specific binding lipid reduces the frequency or spatial amplitude of such events. Overall, the findings provide evidence that p40Phox PX domain possesses a search mechanism involving electrostatic hopping that speeds its acquisition of target lipid, as previously observed for PH domains. The evidence indicates that the autophagy lipid kinase also exhibits electrostatic hopping/skating behavior that is proposed to play a functional role by speeding regulatory encounters with autophagy lipid kinase activators and effectors. Moreover, the ability of the lipid kinase to spontaneously dock to anionic membranes without a target lipid could facilitate its distribution across broad regions of the growing autophagosome. Finally, the autophagy lipid kinase exhibits multiple translational modes that we hypothesize are enabled by its two membrane docking feet.

items.title: MaCADEMIA: a software toolbox for single-molecule fluorescence image quantification
items.abstract_or_text: Single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) is a powerful tool in molecular and cellular biology and part of the broad umbrella of super-resolution microscopy. A distinct feature of SMLM, is its capacity for deep quantification, beyond just spatial information, to copy number, stoichiometry, molecular interaction and dynamics in living cells. The hardware required is increasingly straightforward to implement. However, complexity remains in the image analysis where much remains fragmented across specialised software tools. Here, we present MaCADEMIA (Matlab Computational Analysis of Diffusion, Emitter Molecular Intensity and Abundance), a simple yet powerful toolbox of MATLAB functions and associated documentation to enable straightforward extraction of quantitative single-molecule information. MaCADEMIA performs ensemble particle detection achieving localisation accuracies down to 0.5 pixels Root mean squared error (RMSE) across wide signal-to-noise (SNR) ranges on standardised particle tracking benchmarks, consistently matching or exceeding the performance of 14 leading methods. Our integrated workflow enables molecular counting and stoichiometry determination through stepwise photobleaching analysis, mobility measurement via mean squared displacement, colocalisaton analysis and absolute protein copy number quantification using three-dimensional cellular models.

items.title: Decision stability of a default docking pipeline: a seed, box-placement, and protomer audit on LIT-PCBA MTORC1
items.abstract_or_text: Agentic and automated drug-discovery workflows increasingly call molecular docking as a black-box subroutine and act on its ranked output, typically from a single run under software defaults. We ask a narrow, operational question: if the same default pipeline is re-run with a different random seed, a slightly displaced search box, or a different input protomer, which decisions-the top-k compounds a downstream agent would advanceactually change? Using AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on the LIT-PCBA MTORC1 target (PDB 4jsx) with a fixed, score-blind panel of 60 ligands (20 actives, 40 inactives), we predeclared the decision rule and the seed and box-placement perturbation axes against a baseline, added a protomer arm whose selection criterion was amended during execution (disclosed with dates), and compared top-12 decision sets as symmetric differences (exits and entries), Jaccard indices, and binary decision changes, with pose quality checked by PoseBusters against the exact receptor used for docking. A positive control (redocking the co-crystallized ligand, symmetry-corrected RMSD 0.647 Å) validated the setup. Changing only the random seed replaced 3 of 12 top-12 members (6/60 binary decisions changed); a 2 Å box shift along x replaced 2, along y replaced 4; protomer changes at pH 7.0 replaced none. Eight ligands accounted for all flips, and the single PoseBustersinvalid pose was also a recurrent flipper. A threeseed majority-vote consensus cost 3× compute, dropped the invalid recurrent flipper, and still disagreed with every individual run; we report it as a priced mitigation with measured residual disagreement, not as certified stabilization. All results concern decision repeatability only: nothing here establishes that any decision set is correct, and a consensus can stabilize a wrong answer. All code, inputs, checkpoints, and negative results are provided in an accompanying archive prepared for the author; no public release has been made.

items.title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Å; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

items.title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
items.abstract_or_text: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

items.title: Low-pass filtering revisited: ramped phase randomization for cryo-EM map comparison and data augmentation
items.abstract_or_text: Conventional low-pass filters attenuate or remove high-frequency Fourier amplitudes but leave the phases intact wherever the amplitude response stays above zero. As a result, fine-scale detail of the original signal can persist beyond the target resolution. A sharp cutoff removes this detail but produces ringing artifacts. To address both limitations, this work introduces ramped phase randomization, which extends a conventional low-pass filter by adding random offsets to Fourier phases that increase smoothly with spatial frequency. For cryo-EM maps, the correlation between a map at the target resolution and an ideal, noiseless map sets the levels of the phase offsets, with a correction for the finite resolution of the input map. On three published map pairs, ramped phase filtering reduced the higher resolution parent's fine detail to a level similar to that of independently determined maps at the lower target resolution, whereas amplitude-only filtering kept the parent's sharp features. The FSCs between the filtered maps and their parents closely resembled those of the experimental maps. The same filter also serves as a data augmentation approach for neural network-based machine learning. With ramped phase randomization, each augmented copy keeps the power spectrum and low-frequency content of the original example but has a different high-frequency pattern. For simulated CryoBench particles of 16 ribosome assembly states, phase augmentation raised mean test accuracy in all 20 combinations of training-set size and latent dimension, by 20.8 percentage points on average (range from 3.3 points to 44.2 points). On two general deep learning benchmarks, mean test accuracy rose from 92.15% to 96.99% with 60 labelled UCI Synthetic Control traces and from 53.44% to 74.27% with 500 labelled noisy MNIST images. The ramped phase randomization is implemented in an open-source Python package, with a companion browser application for interactive visualization of cryo-EM maps and filtering effects.

items.title: Molecular dissection of the ChAHP complex subunits Adnp and Chd4 reveals common and divergent functions in retinal development
items.abstract_or_text: Epigenetic remodelling is thought to regulate the progression of competence states in neural progenitor cells. Here, we examined the functions of the ChAHP chromatin remodelling complex during retinal development. ChAHP consists of the ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeller CHD4, the zinc finger and homeodomain transcription factor ADNP, and the HP1 heterochromatin proteins (Cbx1/3/5). Notably, both CHD4 and ADNP are genetically associated with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), but ChAHP functions in neural development are not fully understood. In the retina, we found that both ADNP and CHD4 proteins were co-expressed ubiquitously in each cell type throughout development, and the two proteins formed a complex in vivo. Next, we generated retina-specific conditional knockouts (cKOs) to both Adnp and Chd4 using the Chx10-Cre driver. We observed phenotypic correspondence and divergence. Developmentally, we observed elevated cell death in both Adnp and Chd4 cKOs, but Adnp cKOs also exhibited deficits in progenitor numbers and proliferation. As a result, mature Adnp cKOs were hypoplastic with reductions in each cell type. We previously described a more complex phenotype in Chd4 cKOs, where cell fates were imbalanced and progenitor proliferation was prolonged, but these features were absent from the Adnp cKO. To understand how ChAHP regulates gene expression, we compared Adnp and Chd4 cKOs via scRNA-seq, which revealed common transcriptional signatures. However, Chd4 cKOs exhibited more severe effects on gene expression in line with its stronger effects on cell fate. We then performed cut&run-seq, which suggested that Adnp and Chd4 are recruited to the same genomic loci - many of which are also occupied by the Ctcf transcription factor. Taken together, our data suggest that ChAHP regulates retinal growth, but that CHD4 has additional ChAHP-independent functions in regulating progenitor fate decisions. These findings point to the idea that during neurogenesis, some brain regions may have greater dependence on ChAHP, and therefore greater vulnerability to genetic mutation.

items.title: The Quagmire of Immunogenicity-Guided Antibody Design: Labels Limit Progress
items.abstract_or_text: Generative sequence-based antibody design is increasingly steered by learned property predictors, so a design objective is only as well specified as the labels behind its oracle. Immunogenicity is among the most clinically consequential properties to condition on, and among the least well specified: the supervisory signal is a single anti-drug-antibody percentage (ADA%) per molecule, aggregated from published trials. To analyze that signal, we first extended and corrected the widely used 217-entry dataset to 231 therapeutics with paired sequences, spanning formats from mouse to fully human. Then, we manually reconstructed the clinical evidence for 110 of them from primary sources. We find that an antibody format lookup outperforms every sequence-based learned predictor on the 231-antibody dataset. Apparent accuracy tracks the format composition of the evaluation split rather than sequence signal. Furthermore, the labels understate their own evidence: molecules labeled at [≤]6 ADA% span up to 86% across trials. We recomputed labels from the trial-level measurements and found that the advantage of the format-based approach disappears, while the sequence-based predictors degrade less under the cohort-weighted mean. We conclude that progress is limited by the label itself, and recommend reporting ADA% at the trial level, treating the target as a distribution rather than a point value, and evaluating against a format-based baseline.

items.title: Umpolung of a Diazo Sulfonyl Fluoride Surrogate Expands Diversity-Oriented Clicking to Cyclopropanes
items.abstract_or_text: Herein, we report the synthesis of a new hypervalent iodine reagent, ((((( tert butyldimethylsilyl)oxy)methyl)sulfonyl)(diazo)methyl)(phenyl)- λ 3-iodaneyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (HIR 3 ), from the Diversity-Oriented Clicking (DOC) hub tert -butyl(((diazomethyl)sulfonyl)methoxy)dimethylsilane ( t Bu-DMSM), thereby reversing the native reactivity of its diazo carbon. Reaction of 3 with nucleophilic silyl enol ethers affords β-diazosulfones in good to excellent yields. Subsequent rhodium-catalysed intramolecular 1,3-C–H insertion provides novel cyclopropanes bearing a masked sulfonyl fluoride group in good to excellent yields and diastereoselectivities. Unmasking of this group enables the late-stage formation of cyclopropyl sulfonyl fluorides, either from the isolated cyclopropanes or through a one-pot, two-step sequence from the βdiazosulfones. We further demonstrate that the major cyclopropane diastereomer undergoes base-mediated epimerisation to afford an otherwise inaccessible diastereomer, which participates in sulfur(VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) reactions to furnish the corresponding sulfonates. Finally, trapping of the intermediate sulfinate with benzyl bromide electrophiles, rather than conversion into the sulfonyl fluoride, provides access to structurally diverse sulfones.

items.title: Intravital single-molecule microscopy reveals protein kinetics in live mammalian tissues
items.abstract_or_text: Quantifying individual protein behavior in living mammalian tissues remains challenging. Here we introduce intravital single-molecule microscopy (iSiMM), an imaging and analysis framework that combines instant structured illumination microscopy guided tissue navigation with highly inclined and laminated optical sheet illumination. In live mice, iSiMM enables single-emitter detection and tracking of endogenously expressed fluorescently tagged proteins at 30 ms per frame. Trajectory-based modeling quantifies diffusion coefficients and model-defined bound and free fractions, while localization-density reconstructions map molecular organization. We illustrate the approach using the actomyosin cytoskeleton, resolving isoform-specific mobility and responses to physiological stimulation and genetic perturbation. Single-molecule detection in pancreas and skeletal muscle, including after in vivo transfection, further demonstrates feasibility across additional tissues and labeling strategies. iSiMM provides a framework for investigating molecular behavior in the physiological context of living mammalian tissues.

items.title: Bioactivity foundation model for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization from sequence data
items.abstract_or_text: Learning from large-scale bioactivity archives is complicated by heterogeneous assay readouts and differences in data reliability. Here we show that a model that predicts probability distributions over binding affinities from sequence data opens model training to vast and diverse troves of heterogeneous bioactivity data. We develop PSICHIC+, a bioactivity foundation model trained on approximately 82 million protein-ligand records using a distributional objective that preserves quantitative resolution while incorporating variation in data reliability. Given a protein sequence and ligand SMILES, PSICHIC+ predicts binding affinity in milliseconds. In zero-shot virtual-screening benchmarks without target-specific training data, it improves enrichment over regression- and classification-based approaches and performs competitively with leading structure-based methods. In lab-in-the-loop campaigns, distribution-guided acquisition improves recovery of high-activity compounds under fixed screening budgets. Combining PSICHIC+ with Boltz-2 improves hit-to-lead affinity prediction over Boltz-2 alone, with mean correlation approaching that of FEP+ on the evaluated benchmarks, without requiring high-resolution protein structures. These results support distributional learning as a scalable approach to using heterogeneous bioactivity data for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization.

items.title: Assessing reinforcement learning and vigor with an online decision-making battery
items.abstract_or_text: Reinforcement learning and vigor are two fundamental aspects of decision-making modulated by dopamine. Although vigor is highly relevant for mood disorders, it has been overlooked by previous batteries characterizing decision-making abilities. We developed a test battery with two RL tasks (RL/working memory, go/no-go task) and two vigor tasks (physical effort discounting, foraging task) and administered it to an online community sample (N = 162). We used computational modeling and factor analysis to identify two factors reflecting RL and vigor. The RL factor reflected participants' general decision-making ability, while vigor corresponded to a motivational propensity to obtain rewards. Both factors demonstrated moderately strong test-retest reliability (ICC(2,1) = .65 and .67, respectively) over a one-to-two-week interval. Moreover, both factors were meaningfully related to self-report scales. The RL and vigor factors were negatively and positively associated with mania, respectively, although further analyses revealed that vigor was not fully independent of RL. Neither factor was significantly associated with depression symptoms. Collectively, we present preliminary evidence that vigor may represent a separate factor from RL in line with the putative dopamine hypothesis, paving the way for future longitudinal assessments of RL and vigor in mood disorders.

items.title: Cell-in-drop genotyping detects megabase-scale loss of heterozygosity as a quantitative marker for CRISPR-Cas9 on-target toxicity
items.abstract_or_text: Targeted DNA double strand breaks catalyzed by CRISPR-Cas9 have been demonstrated to cause megabase-scale segmental deletions and whole chromosome losses in a wide variety of mouse and human cell lines. This raises safety concerns for CRISPR-Cas9 based therapeutics and highlights the need for scalable methods to assess its on-target genotoxicity in clinical contexts. In this report, we present cell-in-drop genotyping, as a high throughput approach that combines single cell encapsulation with droplet-based PCR genotyping of endogenous polymorphisms to detect loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at a targeted chromosome without any genome manipulation. With this approach, we detected megabase scale LOH induced by Cas9 DSBs, mostly frequently by segmental loss. This approach also detected LOH from loss of a critical DNA repair factor, BLM helicase, and LOH induced by other genotoxic conditions, in particular, the chemotherapeutic drugs Paclitaxel and Mitomycin C, which were demonstrated to induce LOH by different mechanisms. A modified version of the assay also captured rare local short range LOH arising from DSB-induced interhomologue recombination. Because it requires no genome manipulation, cell-in-drop genotyping offers a practical, scalable tool for evaluating genotoxic risk of CRISPR-Cas9 and other agents in research and clinical development.

items.title: An agent-built, verified atlas of public spatial transcriptomics shows that breadth across studies drives transfer and reproducibility
items.abstract_or_text: Public spatial transcriptomics data are deposited study by study, in formats that differ from one laboratory to the next, and no resource has yet indexed or verified them as a whole. Here we present SpatialDataAgent-DB, an atlas built from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) by SpatialDataAgent, a workflow in which language-model agents do the work and every output is checked rather than trusted. An assay index covering all 298,179 GEO series identifies 2,411 spatial series, which gives public spatial data an explicit denominator. For each series, an agent writes conversion code instead of editing the data directly, and a frozen, rule-based scorer recomputes every released value from the source files. In a held-out test, the scorer rejected all 1,231 corrupted copies. We also visually reviewed every released sample, including the 4,386 H&E-registered Visium samples of our earlier HESRT release. SpatialDataAgent-DB contains 12,163 samples from 12 platforms and 42 species in a single format, each with its provenance and defect flags. Its 8,211 image-paired samples are 5.9 times as many as in the next image-paired resource, and at least 71% of all samples are absent from five existing catalogues. Without batch correction, sequencing-based samples group by organ more than by platform: with platforms balanced, organ explains 32% of the variance of human pseudobulk profiles and platform 13% (mouse, 47% and 18%). We then used the atlas in two applications. Image-to-expression models trained on it transfer to unseen studies, and their accuracy rises steadily with training data and, at a fixed number of patches, with the number of training studies over the range tested (for H&E, Pearson r gains 0.0056 per doubling of training patches up to 524,288); 11 of 13 forecasts locked in advance were confirmed. Adding studies helps more than adding patches from the same studies, because each study leaves a fingerprint in its images. Intent-based search over the same index assembled 70 single-cell dementia studies, and the replication of disease signatures in held-out studies rose steadily with the number of studies (direction agreement averaged over 28 held-out studies, 63% with one study and 77% with 16). In both applications, performance kept rising with the number of independent studies, which a complete and verified atlas is built to provide.

items.title: Plasma-Enhanced Atomic Layer Deposition and Substrate Engineering of Low-Resistivity Ultrathin MoCx Films for Advanced Interconnect Applications
items.abstract_or_text: As Copper (Cu) interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, conventional tantalum/tantalum nitride (Ta/TaN) liner/barrier layers occupy an increasing fraction of the available interconnect volume and introduce additional electrical resistance because of their relatively high resistivity. Therefore, a key challenge is to develop ultrathin liner/barrier materials that can maintain low resistivity while providing effective Cu diffusion-barrier performance. In this work, we demonstrate MoC x as a liner-free barrier material using plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD). For this PEALD-grown film, cycloheptatriene molybdenum tricarbonyl, (η 6 -C 7 H 8 )Mo(CO) 3 , was first introduced as a precursor to synthesize ultrathin molybdenum carbide (MoC x ) films. The effects of plasma reactants, plasma power, deposition temperature, film thickness, and substrate types were systematically evaluated to clarify how PEALD process conditions and substrate chemistry influence the electrical performance of ultrathin MoC x films. We observed nucleation differences during the growth based on the substrate; MoC x films deposited on Al 2 O 3 consistently exhibited lower resistivity than those grown on SiO 2 . Using the optimized deposition process, amorphous MoC x films thinner than 5 nm showed resistivities as low as ~230 μΩ·cm without any post-deposition annealing. For reference, current Ta/TaN liner/barrier layers typically exceed 500 μΩ·cm resistivity in the sub-5 nm thickness regime. Sub-5 nm MoC x film also showed good Cu adhesion and effective Cu diffusion-barrier behavior after thermal annealing of up to 500 °C. These results demonstrate the potential of ultrathin amorphous MoC x as a low-resistivity liner-free barrier material for advanced Cu interconnects.

items.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

items.title: Production of a resilient biosurfactant using agro-wastes and Paenibacillus dendritiformis isolated from petroleum-contaminated soil: a break-even analysis at pilot scale
items.abstract_or_text: Wastes from mustard oil mills and dairy were used as partial replacement of pure reagents in modified Bushnell and Haas broth media for production of biosurfactant by Paenibacillus dendritiformis isolated from petroleum-contaminated soil. The process was optimised by construction of a response model using Taguchi experimental design, leading to a 28.23% increase in performance characteristics and a 13.23 % increase in yield of biosurfactant. The optimized production medium consisted of carbon @7.9 %, nitrogen @ 1.1% and agitation rate 180 r.p.m. This was provided by adding glucose @ 2%, ammonium nitrate @0.2%, mustard oil seed meal @10% and whey@ 10% in modified Bushnell Haas broth. The biosurfactant produced retained its properties during exposure to a wide range of pH values (5-11), high temperatures (up to 121C), high salinities of up to 5% and also five -fold concentration. Approximately three- fold increase in yield of the biosurfactant (25g/L to 68.5g/L) was obtained upon scaling-up the production from 100ml to 1500 ml in a lab scale fermenter with agitation @ 150r.p.m. and D.O. levels maintained at 6mg/L. Power calculations and the cost thereof was calculated (Rs 10.24 /L) and summed up with the cost of raw materials Rs 8.40/L and found to be Rs 18.64/L of product .Since 68.5g product is present in 1L, the cost is calculated to be Rs 271/- per kg. Comparison with selling price of currently used chemical surfactants like Linear Alkyl Benzene sulphonic acid (LAB) and sodium Lauryl sulphate and Sodium Lauryl ether sulphate (SLS and SLES) reveals that prices of these products varies from Rs 120 to 600 per kg depending on manufacturer and quality, order quantity. From the above studies it can be seen that production and use of this multiutility biosurfactant has, besides a clear advantage over chemically produced surfactants in terms of sustainability, a fairly good comparison with selling price of currently used chemical surfactants. The present study on the production costs (excluding capital costs) successfully demonstrates a break even analysis into the production of biosurfactants.

items.title: Exciton Diffusion Drives Efficiency Roll-off in TADF OLEDs
items.abstract_or_text: 2 Abstract Despite their potential to deliver high-efficiency organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), those using thermally activated delayed fluorescent (TADF) emitters often suffer from a large drop in efficiency at high luminance. This effect is known as efficiency roll-off and is a longstanding issue for these devices, which has limited their commercial deployment. We have discovered that the degree of overlap between the photoluminescence (PL) and absorption spectra drives singlet exciton diffusion and is a strong predictor of the magnitude of efficiency roll-off in TADF OLEDs. This effect is especially important in OLEDs made with multiresonant (MR)-TADF materials given their intense low-energy short-range charge transfer absorption bands. MR-TADF OLEDs are very appealing due to their narrow emission spectra; however, their small Stokes shift leads to large spectral overlap and contributes to these devices showing severe efficiency roll-off. Developing TADF materials that have a larger Stokes shift whilst maintaining their bright, narrow emission would help minimize efficiency roll-off while securing high internal quantum efficiencies, features particularly relevant for displays.

items.title: SMFnet reveals principles of combinatorial transcription factor assembly
items.abstract_or_text: Combinatorial assembly of transcription factors (TFs) opens chromatin at cis-regulatory elements (cREs) to establish cell-type-specific gene expression. Dissecting the role of individual TFs and their collective function has been limited by the diversity of TF binding-site arrangements across cREs. A single regulatory sequence can support multiple configurations of TF and nucleosome occupancy, raising the possibility that distinct chromatin states reflect different TF assemblies. Predictive models linking regulatory sequence to chromatin accessibility collapse these distinct molecular states into population averages, obscuring how TF assemblies shape accessible chromatin. Here, we introduce SMFNet, a generative diffusion model that predicts distributions of single-molecule chromatin accessibility profiles from DNA sequence, and PRISM, which identifies sequence features associated with individual molecular states. Together, these approaches enable us to systematically associate single molecule chromatin states at cREs with specific TF binding motifs. Experimental perturbation of these motifs redistributes the corresponding states as predicted by SMFNet, supporting their interpretation as TF-dependent configurations underlying chromatin opening. We then use controlled in silico motif screens to systematically dissect individual and combinatorial TF contributions to chromatin opening. Individual TFs show distinct chromatin-opening signatures, differing in accessible-region width and nucleosome-positioning precision even when associated with similar levels of chromatin accessibility. Combining motifs reveals partner- and spacing-dependent effects on chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy and nucleosome positioning. Genetic perturbation of TF binding sites using natural variation at endogenous cRE confirms that TF-specific properties shape chromatin accessibility in vivo. Together, our findings reveal sequence-encoded principles of combinatorial TF assembly during chromatin opening.

items.title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility
items.abstract_or_text: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis-regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

items.title: Quantitative imaging of native tissue architecture combined with deep multi-omics reveals the spatial biology of kidney aging
items.abstract_or_text: Aging alters tissue architecture and metabolism in spatially heterogeneous ways, yet the connections between these measurable structural and compositional phenotypes and underlying molecular changes are largely unknown. Here, we introduce NORIGAMI (NoRI-Guided AI for Multimodal Integration), a pipeline combining Normalized Raman Imaging (NoRI), deep learning, quantitative morphology, deep proteomics, and metabolomics to investigate renal aging. Unlike conventional histology, NoRI provides label-free, scattering-corrected measurements of absolute total protein and lipid mass concentrations (mg/mL). In 32 male rats aged 9, 18, 21 and 25 months, NORIGAMI predicted the chronological age of held-out rats from NoRI images (mean absolute error 0.78 months; R^2 = 0.97), and whole-tissue images outperformed models trained on isolated tubules. Quantitative imaging identified 41 age-associated morphological and compositional features (FDR < 0.05), revealing anatomically heterogeneous and non-linear changes in lipid droplet concentration, droplet size, cytoplasmic lipid concentration and tubular architecture. Deep molecular profiling quantified 11,485 proteins and 269 metabolites, revealing coordinated declines in differentiated proximal tubule (PT) identity and oxidative metabolism, selective increases in basement-membrane collagen-IV chains, and increasing molecular heterogeneity with age. A protein clock, built mainly from extracellular-matrix and heparan-sulfate proteins, predicted age with a mean absolute error of 1.6 months. Old kidneys diverged along a dominant injury-remodeling axis, seen separately in the proteome, in kidney RNA from 54 other rats and in the metabolome, in which tubular-injury and immune proteins, including the NAD+ consuming enzyme CD38, rise as differentiated-tubule proteins and NAD+ fall. NORIGAMI subsequently linked NAD+ associated molecular changes to quantitative features of tubular geometry and protein-lipid organization, while complementary KIM-1-centered analyses identified overlapping morphological associations involving epithelial injury and lipid handling and yielded additional molecular candidates for mechanistic validation. Collectively, these findings suggest that declining tubular metabolic function, altered lipid organization and injury-associated molecular programs represent interconnected features of renal aging. NORIGAMI establishes a framework for identifying the quantitative structural manifestations of molecular aging and generating spatially informed, experimentally testable hypotheses about tissue dysfunction.

items.title: Fertilization offsets the maternal age effect on mouse oocytes provided the oviduct is not itself aged
items.abstract_or_text: Advanced maternal age compromises oocyte quality, and it is widely assumed that these deficits are transmitted to embryos. However, because most studies rely on in vivo conception, it has been difficult to separate the effects of oocyte aging from those of an aged fertilization environment. In aging mice, we observed that the fraction of ovulated oocytes forming implantation sites after in vivo conception fell ~3.7-fold, raising the question of whether this was due to reduced fertilization, reduced embryo quality or reduced support from the aged reproductive tract. Therefore we fertilized oocytes of aged and young mice in vitro with a shared young-donor sperm preparation, holding the fertilization environment constant and removing paternal variability. Hallmarks of maternal age were largely offset following fertilization in vitro: aged oocytes produced blastocysts at rates comparable to young controls, with altered - but not deficient - cell-lineage composition and no detectable impairment in development to term (E18.5) after transfer to young oviducts. Proteomic analysis revealed that, unlike the transcriptomic signature, the proteomic age signature of oocytes was not faithfully propagated to the blastocyst: for a subset of proteins, particularly those depleted in aged oocytes, the direction of the age effect reversed between oocyte and blastocyst. Comparison with parthenogenetically activated oocytes showed this divergence to be fertilization-dependent, implicating fertilization - rather than mere embryonic cleavage - as the driver of proteomic change. Stable-isotope labelling in live embryos showed that blastocysts from aged, fertilized oocytes both synthesized more new protein and retained less maternal protein than young counterparts; neither effect was detectable after parthenogenesis. Puromycin labelling, by contrast, showed a maternal-age-associated rise in bulk synthesis regardless of route.
