Together, these results indicate that the maternal-age effect on the oocyte proteome is labile rather than fixed and can be offset by fertilization itself, provided the maternal environment is not itself aged.

items.title: BRIDGE: Biological Antimicrobial Resistance Inference via Domain-Knowledge Graph Embeddings
items.abstract_or_text: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global health crisis, responsible for an estimated 1.27 million deaths in 2019 alone. Traditional approaches to identifying antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) are often labour-intensive and limited in their ability to detect novel resistance mechanisms. In this study, we propose BRIDGE, a knowledge graph-based framework, to improve AMR gene prediction by integrating gene neighbourhood information and protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. Focusing on Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli, we con- struct a comprehensive and biologically grounded knowl- edge graph using curated data from CARD, STRING, and DrugBank. We apply knowledge graph embedding models which are fed into neural networks to infer novel AMR links, achieving classification accuracy of up to 97%. Our results demonstrate that incorporating biologically meaningful re- lationships, such as gene neighbourhood information and PPIs, enhances the predictive accuracy and interpretability of AMR link predictions. This work contributes to the de- velopment of scalable and data-integrated approaches for advancing antimicrobial resistance surveillance and drug discovery. BRIDGE implementation and data are available at https://github.com/GraphML-lab/BRIDGE.

items.title: HNRNPC-mediated RNA processing promotes VHL-associated excessive vasculogenesis in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome revealed from patient-derived blood vessel models
items.abstract_or_text: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome (VHLS) is an inherited disorder characterized by excessive vascularization, which contributes to the development of hemangioblastomas and benign or malignant tumors, as well as renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and cysts in multiple organs. VHLS is caused by mutations in VHL tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Although therapeutic agents targeting hypoxia-inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF2A), which is stabilized by VHL loss and promotes tumor angiogenesis, have been approved for clinical use, their therapeutic response remains limited in RCC patients associated with VHLS. Therefore, there is an unmet need for the development of alternative therapeutic approaches independent of HIF2A. Here, we establish a human iPSCs-based model of VHLS-associated excessive vasculogenesis using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from VHLS patients and VHL-edited isogenic iPSC lines. Vascular cells (VCs) differentiated from these VHLS-specific iPSCs exhibited excessive blood vessel formation compared to healthy donor-derived VCs, leading to vascular lesion formation characterized by abundant blood vessels and abnormal cellular growth in vivo. Mechanistically, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were preferentially stabilized in the patient-VCs. Among these RBPs, the stabilization of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (HNRNPC), which is a substrate for pVHL-mediated protein degradation independent of HIF2A expression, was critical for the dysregulated vascularization caused by VHL inactivation in this model. These findings provide an iPSCs-derived vascular platform to elucidate VHLS mechanisms and identify HNRNPC as a potential therapeutic target for VHL-driven vascular lesion formations through an HIF2A-independent mechanism.

items.title: Formation Energy is All You Need
items.abstract_or_text: A Pourbaix diagram maps which species of an element (metal, ion, oxide or hydroxide) is thermodynamically stable in water as a function of potential and pH, at fixed temperature, pressure and composition. Constructing one requires the Gibbs energies of formation of the participating phases and species. Obtaining reliable values, however, remains difficult: competing phases and species can differ by only a few kilojoules per mole, while published compilations may disagree and are not always freely reusable. Density functional theory (DFT) offers an alternative, but its errors can exceed the energy differences that determine phase stability. We introduce pourbase, an open, source-linked thermodynamic database with a Python package and desktop application for constructing Pourbaix diagrams. Individual reported values, their provenance and a configurable selection policy are accessible and configurable to users even while the database expands as agent-guided literature searches collect new data. We show that replacing a single formation energy can substantially change a predicted stability region and that established thermodynamic compilations can yield conflicting oxide stability boundaries. By making thermodynamic data accessible, traceable, and revisable, pourbase enables reproducible Pourbaix diagrams built directly from experimental evidence, as well as a platform for benchmarking computed values, as we demonstrate for the Materials Project, against experimental values. Ultimately, accurate phase stability predictions need not depend on increasingly complex models, but on getting the formation energies right.

items.title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
items.abstract_or_text: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

items.title: QuantCell: machine learning based cell annotation integrating qualitative and quantitative imaging profiles
items.abstract_or_text: Recent advances in spatial omics enable high-resolution, multiplexed imaging of RNA and protein expression, but cell annotation remains challenging, particularly in complex tissues with numerous markers or rare cell types. Here, we present QuantCell, a machine learning framework that leverages quantitative imaging data to improve annotation derived from qualitative profiles. QuantCell evaluates multiple models and applies a user-defined false discovery rate to ensure high-confidence annotation. Using PhenoCycler imaging of mouse bone marrow, QuantCell increased annotated cells from 33.1% to 90.2% at 5% FDR, achieving 96.5% accuracy. QuantCell supports diverse imaging platforms and robustly detects rare cell populations.

items.title: Glutamine antagonism suppresses tumor growth in adrenocortical carcinoma through inhibition of de novo nucleotide biosynthesis
items.abstract_or_text: Dysregulation of cellular metabolism is a hallmark of cancer, which remains poorly understood in adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC). Here, we dissected ACC metabolism by integrating transcriptional profiling from human and mouse ACC, targeted tissue metabolomics from a mouse ACC model, and untargeted serum metabolomics from a large patient cohort, providing cross-species validation of metabolic rewiring in ACC. This study revealed global metabolic dysregulation, involving glutamine-dependent pathways such as amino-acid and hexosamine biosynthesis, nucleotide metabolism, and glutathione biosynthesis, suggesting glutamine catabolism is a critical metabolic vulnerability in ACC. Treatment with glutamine antagonists 6-Diazo-5-Oxo-L-Norleucine (DON) and JHU-083 elicited robust anti-tumor responses. Mechanistic studies revealed DON's anti-tumor effect was primarily driven by selective inhibition of glutamine-fueled de novo nucleotide biosynthesis. Additionally, DON led to DNA damage, which yielded potent synergism with inhibition of the DNA damage response pathway. Collectively, this work highlights glutamine metabolism as a central metabolic dependency and therapeutic target in ACC.

items.title: Single-cell foundation models transfer across deep evolutionary distances
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell foundation models are trained mostly on human and other vertebrate cells, yet are proposed as general-purpose models. Whether they transfer far beyond their training species is unknown. We evaluated zero-shot embeddings from Geneformer, scGPT and UCE against PCA and scVI in developmental atlases of Dictyostelium discoideum and Caenorhabditis elegans, separated from humans by 1.2 billion and 600 million years. Without retraining, the models recovered developmental order and preserved organism-specific cell identities. UCE encodes genes by protein sequence and could use 97% of measured genes, whereas Geneformer and scGPT, after ortholog mapping, used under one-fifth. UCE performed most consistently, often exceeding species-native baselines. Restricted to ortholog-mappable genes, it still scored above vocabulary-based models on five of six annotation tasks, some narrowly. Foundation models can thus yield informative cell embeddings across more than a billion years of evolution, and protein-sequence gene representations make these embeddings more complete and often more accurate.

items.title: BMP4 Restricts Axonal Ramification and Bouton Density in Cholinergic Projections from the Basal Forebrain
items.abstract_or_text: Axonal projections and precise synapse formation are essential for the establishment of functional neural circuits, and their dysregulation contributes to various psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Although numerous extracellular cues secreted from surrounding tissues regulate axon guidance and synapse formation, the mechanisms by which neurons locally regulate terminal patterning within their projection fields remain poorly understood. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) is a classical morphogen that is involved in early neural tube patterning during development. However, its postnatal function remains unclear. Previous in vitro studies using hippocampal glutamatergic neurons demonstrated that BMP4 can act locally on axons to suppress synapse formation, raising the possibility that BMP4 regulates terminal differentiation after target innervation. Here, we investigated the role of BMP4 in postnatal cholinergic circuit development using cholinergic neuron-specific Bmp4 conditional knockout (Bmp4 cKO) mice, with adult analyses performed in males. Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons project extensively throughout the neocortex and are essential for higher brain functions, including arousal and attention. Bmp4 cKO mice exhibited increased cholinergic axon terminals in the neocortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, as well as increased axonal ramification in the neocortex without affecting cytoarchitectonic organization or cholinergic neuron numbers in the basal forebrain. These findings demonstrate that BMP4 functions as a negative regulator of cholinergic terminal formation and axonal arborization, suggesting that BMP4 may act locally to restrict cholinergic axonal expansion during neural circuit maturation.

items.title: Direct Access to α-Aryl-β-Amino Aldehydes via Hypervalent Iodine-Mediated Oxidative Rearrangement of Cinnamyl Amines
items.abstract_or_text: Selective synthesis of α-aryl-β-amino aldehydes remains less developed despite considerable progress in Mannich reactions, aza-Michael additions and asymmetric hydroformylation. Here we report a phenyliodine(III) bis(trifluoroacetate) (PIFA)-mediated oxidative rearrangement of cinnamyl amines through formal 1,2-aryl migration. The reaction proceeds at 0 °C under ambient air and accommodates diverse nitrogen substituents, migrating aryl groups and pharmaceutical-derived substrates. A 6-gram preparation and subsequent transformations to β-amino acids, 1,3-amino alcohols, 1,3-diamines and azetidines, together with the synthesis of a valifenalate isomer, demonstrate the synthetic utility of the aldehyde products. Mechanistic experiments suggest a pathway involving a bis(trifluoroacetate) intermediate. An initial asymmetric variant using chiral iodine(III) reagents furnished a celecoxib-derived chiral aldehyde, with up to 77% ee measured for its reduced chiral alcohol derivative.

items.title: Psychedelics restructure information in the human brain
items.abstract_or_text: How do psychedelic drugs alter human brain function? Answering this question relies on our ability to understand how information is stored, transferred, and transformed across the cortex. Here, we leverage a precise mathematical framework for multivariate information decomposition to construct the first comprehensive picture of these processes across five compounds: LSD, psilocybin, ketamine, DMT and 5-MeO-DMT (N=80). We provide a formal and empirical explanation of major prior results, revealing sets of competing underlying phenomena masked by extant approaches. We extend this analysis to novel higher-order phenomena, and we demonstrate how all of these observations can emerge from a minimal generative model in which neural populations operate with reduced self-coupling. In sum, our results suggest that the psychedelic brain is one in which cortical populations become alike, but not necessarily together. This has important implications for models of how psychedelics reorganize brain dynamics to alter subjective experience and alleviate mental health conditions.

items.title: RegEvol: detection of directional selection in regulatory sequences through phenotypic predictions and phenotype-to-fitness functions
items.abstract_or_text: Regulatory DNA controls when and where genes are expressed, making it a key driver of phenotypic evolution. Yet detecting selection in non-coding regions remains difficult, as most approaches rely on sequence conservation or changes in substitution rate rather than molecular effects. RegEvol bridges this gap by linking machine learning-based predictions of transcription factor binding to explicit evolutionary models. It uses the distribution of predicted mutational effects to infer fitness functions under different evolutionary scenarios including random drift, stabilising selection, and directional selection. Through maximum-likelihood estimation, it identifies the regime that best explains observed changes along a lineage from an ancestral sequence. When substitution numbers are limited, such as along short evolutionary branches, likelihood differences can be aggregated across sets of regulatory elements to increase statistical power. RegEvol corrects biases that affected previous tests based on machine learning of transcription factor binding, while remaining conservative across different levels of divergence. Applied to over 3 million Drosophila melanogaster regulatory regions, we identify 5.1% under directional selection, enriched near reproductive and immune genes. Applying the aggregation strategy to human CTCF binding across tissues reveals enrichment of directional signals in nervous and male reproductive systems. The framework is readily applicable to experimentally detected regulatory elements with alignable ancestral sequences and is flexible to future advances in understanding regulatory function, providing a powerful basis for investigating adaptation in non-coding regions.

items.title: Feedback reliability modulates learning-related dynamics of midfrontal error monitoring
items.abstract_or_text: Learning from feedback requires the brain to evaluate both performance outcomes and the reliability of the information used for learning. This study examined the dynamics of neural performance monitoring during deterministic (100% reliable) and probabilistic (75% reliable) associative learning using two within-subject tasks with different stimulus materials. Behavioral performance improved under both feedback regimes, but learning was consistently more successful under deterministic feedback. Error-related negativity, feedback-related negativity, and phase-locked midfrontal theta became progressively more pronounced across deterministic learning, particularly in the image-image task, whereas corresponding changes were attenuated under probabilistic feedback. Induced theta showed the opposite pattern, decreasing across deterministic learning while remaining comparatively stable under probabilistic learning. These opposing theta trajectories suggest that phase-locked and induced activity reflect distinct components of learning-related neural adaptation that may be obscured when total theta power is considered alone. Overall, the findings indicate that feedback reliability shapes the progressive tuning of midfrontal performance-monitoring responses during learning.

items.title: Uncovering disease progression trajectories across multiple timescales with hybrid ODE-mixture models
items.abstract_or_text: Biological systems are capable of evolving across multiple timescales, yet most modeling approaches capture either short-term physiological responses or long-term disease progression. Additionally, methods that combine these time scales either struggle with inter-individual variation, or require large volumes of data to work. We present Latent Class Parameter Trajectory Analysis (LCPTA), a hybrid framework that combines mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE) modeling of short-term dynamics with latent class trajectory modeling of long-term parameter evolution. To support this approach, we developed TemporalMixtureModels.jl, a Julia package for univariate and multivariate temporal mixture modeling. We evaluated LCPTA in two synthetic longitudinal studies, covering a simulation of a heterogeneous population developing hypertension, as well as a synthetic longitudinal study of 75 virtual individuals followed over 30 years, representing muscle insulin resistance, liver insulin resistance, and healthy trajectories. We compared LCPTA with a conditional neural ODE and a conditional neural network for reconstruction of long-term parameter trajectories and subgroup separation. In both studies LCPTA recovered relevant subgroup structure and trajectory patterns. In the cardiovascular study, the neural approaches were able to distinguish inter-individual differences, but in the insulin sensitivity study, neural approaches failed to represent parameter trajectories faithfully, primarily separating individuals along a single dominant parameter and showing weaker multivariate trajectory reconstruction. In additional experiments with sparse and irregularly sampled unseen individuals, LCPTA maintained strong classification performance. We show that LCPTA is an efficient and interpretable strategy for multiscale modeling of heterogeneous metabolic disease progression, with potential utility for data-efficient digital twin applications.

items.title: Negative effects of oxygen and halogen species on charge extraction in perovskite solar cells with fullerene electron transport layers
items.abstract_or_text: In this work, we explore the effect of small molecular species such as air, iodide, iodine, and triiodide species on the charge transport behavior of fullerene electron transport layers and the concomitant effects on performance and stability of perovskite solar cells. First, we show that without SnOx buffer layers, two-step vapor deposited perovskites have notable losses upon air exposure while spin-coated perovskites have minor losses. We hypothesize that these effects are caused by intrinsic organohalide excess in the CSS perovskite film, leading to an enrichment of mobile halide species such as iodide, iodine, and polyiodides, coupled with a deterioration of C60 charge transport properties. We show that the fill factor losses found in two-step vapor-deposited devices upon air exposure can be induced in spin-coated perovskites by treating their surface with potassium triiodide solutions, further implicating polyhalide species in these losses. Drift-diffusion simulations support the hypothesis that this may be explained by deep electron traps in the C60 formed by polyhalides, while O2 may form shallower traps that have more minor effects on device performance in isolation. Critically, we identify that common ammonium halide surface passivation treatments can lead to performance losses with similar current-voltage signatures during operation in time periods as short as 30 minutes. This may be caused by in situ iodine and polyhalide generation from photolysis of residual lead iodide reducing charge extraction in these solar cells. This work has important implications for the design of stable perovskite solar cells with fullerene charge transport layers.

items.title: Surfactant-Toolkit and SurfBench-200: an open computation toolkit and a benchmark of tool-augmented language-model reasoning in surfactant science

items.title: Batch Effect Correction to Enhance Utility of a Publicly Available ALS Proteomics Dataset
items.abstract_or_text: Large, publicly available databases of patient data have been successful in identifying associations between neurodegenerative diseases and biological features that might otherwise go unnoticed. The Answer ALS Consortium is one such database that has generated a rich repository of multi-omic data from people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, large studies can suffer from batch effects that obscure genuine biological signal and prevent experiment reproducibility. In this study, we identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS 1-2 proteomic dataset (508 samples x 3,643 proteins) and corrected the effect using both the internal controls provided by Answer ALS and the batch effect-correction algorithm (BECA) ComBat. We identified a batch effect in the Answer ALS Dataset 1-2 proteomic dataset that, uncorrected, may obscure biology. Proteins MOS and H4 were outliers of expression in the dataset that correlated with the batch effect. Removing MOS and H4 did not correct the effect fully but did reveal new principal component (PC) contributing proteins related to motor neurons and potentially ALS: AINX, NFL, and NFM. The batch differential controls (BDCs) provided by Answer ALS were used to correct samples in their respective batches. ComBat, a well-characterized BECA, was applied to the dataset both before (ComBat-BDC) and after (BDC-ComBat) correction with the BDCs. BDC-ComBat was the only method that successfully reduced batch effect across the entire dataset. This method also preserved four of the top six PC-contributing proteins from the original dataset, including three neuronal proteins, suggesting that the corrected dataset recapitulates biology as well as the variability of the original dataset. Altogether, we produced a version of the Answer ALS proteomic dataset (354 samples by 3,641 proteins) with globally reduced batch effect and protein-level reduced batch effect. This version of the dataset recapitulates the individual protein variability and important neuronal proteins of the original. We also created a workflow for identifying and correcting batch effects that can be applied to other large data repositories.
